practice: Prescribed or rotational grazing with cross-fencing

note: Plan: no single E. coli percentage; response depends on stocking, timing, and wildlife sources

practice: Livestock exclusion fencing (riparian areas and washes)
funding_guide: Erosion control or stream stabilization; Riparian restoration

practice: Hardened or limited livestock crossing

practice: Heavy use area protection (hardened surfaces at corrals and water sites)

note: Plan: 9-89% fecal coliform reduction; use conservatively

practice: Range seeding and critical area planting
priority_area: Disturbed uplands in McElmo, Chinle, and lower Montezuma
note: Plan: 22-100% sediment reduction for cover and revegetation, depending on establishment. Rated at year 5

practice: Pinyon-juniper and brush management with seeding
priority_area: Mancos Shale uplands; Spring Creek and Montezuma Bench near Monticello
note: Added: runoff and erosion control on encroached rangeland; fuelwood benefit

practice: Range or conservation management plan
priority_area: Grazing allotments in priority areas
note: Carries KWRI R-14 plan ratings

practice: Corral relocation away from washes, with runoff controls (sheep, horse, and cattle corrals)
priority_area: Montezuma Creek; Aneth; San Juan corridor
tracking_unit: Number of corrals moved or controlled
note: NRCS 313, 561, 634 (small animal feeding operation practices in Utah NPS plan Appendix A). Larger herds than H-9 backyard pens.

practice: Cheatgrass and annual weed treatment with reseeding
priority_area: Mesas and Abajo foothills
note: NRCS 315. Best fit on mesas and Abajo foothills; in the low desert, red brome and Russian thistle matter more. Added benefit: lower fire risk.

practice: Wind erosion control on rangeland: sand fence, brush barriers, and native seeding on dunes and blowouts
priority_area: Sand sheets and dunes on the Navajo Nation; Aneth and Montezuma Creek uplands
note: Brush and sand fences trap moving sand so seeded plants can establish. Planting risk applies; works only with grazing rest. Also cuts dust from disturbed and mine-affected ground.

practice: Earthen stock tanks and charcos: cleanout, spillway repair, and fencing
funding_guide: Livestock watering trough; Check dams or sediment control
priority_area: Grazed uplands on the Navajo Nation, Montezuma, and Recapture
note: NRCS 378 (pond). Common across the watershed; traps sediment and keeps livestock off streams, but tanks silt in and spillways breach in big storms. Discount 35%: below new earthen structures (50%) because work armors the spillway; above low rock structures. Evaporation loses water.

practice: Hillslope contour rock lines, trincheras, and rock mulch
priority_area: Mancos Shale and sandstone slopes above incised washes
note: Upland rock work that slows sheet and rill flow before it reaches the wash. Ancestral Puebloan terraces and check walls on Cedar Mesa are local precedent. Hand-built with local rock and crews.

practice: One-rock dams and baffles and media lunas
priority_area: Incised gullies in Mancos Shale landscapes (Chinle, McElmo)
tracking_unit: Structures installed or channel length treated
note: Plan: about 50% of sediment retained over 4 years (AZ) and 60-67% more aggradation (NM); failure discount still applied. Cost from Borderlands Restoration Network (about $65 per medium structure in 2019). Post-fire BMP tool: rock structures hold up better than wood in dry settings

practice: Zuni and Navajo bowls and rock rundowns (headcut control)
funding_guide: Check dams or sediment control; Erosion control or stream stabilization
priority_area: Incised gullies in Mancos Shale landscapes (Chinle, McElmo)

practice: Loose-rock check dams and gully plugs over one rock high
priority_area: Incised gullies in Mancos Shale landscapes (Chinle, McElmo)
tracking_unit: Structures installed or channel length treated
note: Failure evidence: Zuni Reservation and Arizona surveys. Post-fire BMP tool: rock structures hold up better than wood in dry settings

practice: Beaver dam analogs and post-assisted log structures
priority_area: Bears Ears canyons; Abajo headwater and meadow reaches
tracking_unit: Structures installed or stream length treated
note: Plan: about 2.3 C summer cooling and up to 0.33 m water table rise in the first year in analogous systems. Needs water rights check

practice: Streambank stabilization with bioengineering (willow and cottonwood poles, toe wood)
priority_area: Montezuma Creek reaches with confirmed bank erosion
note: Willow and cottonwood poles and toe wood. Scored for concentrated storm flow: wood and poles are often scoured out by flash floods before roots take hold, so the wood discount (30%) applies.

practice: Native riparian planting (cottonwood, willow, shrubs) on floodplain terraces with spread-out runoff
priority_area: San Juan riparian corridor; spring-fed canyon streams; private irrigated lands
tracking_unit: Stream miles or riparian acres restored
note: Plan: 40-70% sediment reduction where runoff arrives as sheet flow; about 0.6 C summer cooling from shade. Needs early watering and browse protection

practice: Native riparian planting (cottonwood, willow, shrubs) in washes, with concentrated storm flow
priority_area: Lower Montezuma and Recapture Creeks; Bears Ears canyons; San Juan corridor washes
tracking_unit: Stream miles or riparian acres restored
note: Where flow concentrates, buffers treat only 6-81% of their area and trap 15-43% of sediment versus 41-99% under sheet flow (Helmers and others 2008). Pair with structures that spread flow first

practice: Native riparian seeding (grasses, sedges, rushes, forbs) on wash margins and floodplains
priority_area: San Juan riparian corridor; spring-fed canyon streams
note: NRCS 390 and 342. Utah BMP Selector UT-SB-09 (its second-highest practice). Rarely establishes in washes without grazing rest and flow slowing; score as a pair where possible.

practice: Tamarisk and Russian olive removal with revegetation
priority_area: San Juan River corridor near Navajo Nation lands and recreation areas
note: Plan: cannot assume hydrologic improvement from removal alone. Retreatment needed; flycatcher habitat review

practice: Sediment or settling basin
priority_area: Lower Montezuma Creek; below mineralized ground
note: Metals rating assumes siting below mineralized ground. In-wash basins are earthen embankments, so the earthen discount (50%) applies. Selenium is mostly dissolved and does not settle.

practice: Wetland restoration in canyon bottoms
priority_area: Bears Ears canyons; springs and wetlands
note: Canyon-bottom wetlands take the full force of concentrated storm flow, so the low-structure discount (15%) applies. Where inflow carries selenium, birds can take it up.

practice: Vegetated filter strips at field edges and uplands, with spread-out runoff
priority_area: San Juan River recreation reaches (Bluff to Mexican Hat); lower Montezuma Creek
tracking_unit: Buffer acres established or stream miles buffered
note: Plan: 43-74% fecal coliform trapping and 40-70% sediment where runoff is diffuse. Not a substitute for livestock exclusion or septic fixes

practice: Vegetated filter strips along washes, with concentrated storm flow
priority_area: Washes below fields and corrals in lower Montezuma Creek and McElmo
tracking_unit: Buffer acres established or stream miles buffered
note: Where flow concentrates, buffers treat only 6-81% of their area and trap 15-43% of sediment versus 41-99% under sheet flow (Helmers and others 2008). Pair with structures that spread flow first

practice: Woven brush dams and brush weirs (juniper, willow, or other local brush)
funding_guide: Check dams or sediment control; Erosion control or stream stabilization
priority_area: Incised washes and fields on Navajo Nation lands; Mancos Shale landscapes
note: Traditional Dine and Zuni practice. Black Mesa work reports up to 28% more downstream water and a month longer flow; at Zuni, 5 of 28 brush structures needed maintenance after 20 years. Ratings to be confirmed with chapter practitioners. Discount set at 20%: brush is wood, but the Zuni record (5 of 28 needing maintenance after 20 years) shows it holds better than log structures.

practice: Log and juniper slash piles in washes and gullies
funding_guide: Check dams or sediment control; Pinyon-juniper management
priority_area: Incised washes below pinyon-juniper treatments; Spring Creek and Montezuma Bench
note: Uses slash from pinyon-juniper thinning. The post-fire BMP tool scores log structures low where rainfall is under 10 inches, so the wood discount applies

practice: Log and rock vanes to direct flow away from eroding banks
priority_area: Montezuma Creek and canyon streams with eroding banks
note: Post-fire BMP tool: channel deflectors and native rock score moderately to well in dry settings; rock holds up better than wood. Log or rock vanes in the channel take concentrated flow; wood discount (30%) applies.

practice: Wool mat buffers and wool erosion blankets
priority_area: Disturbed slopes and wash margins; post-fire slopes
note: Montana roadside trials: wool blankets grew 3-4 times more perennial grass than straw or coir, likely from moisture retention and nitrogen. Can use local Navajo-Churro wool; ratings to be confirmed locally. Scored for wash margins: mats can be displaced or buried by concentrated storm flow, so a 25% discount applies.

practice: Waterspreading: low dikes and spreaders that spread wash flow onto rangeland
priority_area: Valley bottoms below washes in Chinle, McElmo, and Montezuma Creek (Navajo Nation lands)
note: NRCS 640; listed in Utah NPS plan Appendix A. Close to traditional Diné floodwater spreading. Low earthen spreaders breach in large flows; discount set at 25% (between earthen and low-structure risk) because spreaders are low and flow is spread, not ponded. On Mancos Shale, spreading more water into the soil can mobilize salt and selenium; site soils should be checked.

practice: Floodplain reconnection: removing berms and spoil piles and setting back levees
priority_area: Lower Montezuma Creek; San Juan corridor
note: Lets floods spread and drop sediment on the floodplain instead of cutting the channel deeper. Needs Clean Water Act section 404 permits and agreement from neighboring landowners.

practice: Unpaved road drainage (rolling dips and culverts and low-water crossings)
priority_area: BLM and county roads connected to channels in McElmo, Chinle, and lower Montezuma
tracking_unit: Road miles treated or drainage features installed
note: Low-water crossings and culverts sit in the wash, so the low-structure discount applies.

practice: Road, two-track, and off-road route closure and decommissioning (including routes in washes)
priority_area: BLM and county roads connected to channels in McElmo, Chinle, and lower Montezuma
note: Loss of access is the main tradeoff

practice: Road surfacing: graveled travel way
priority_area: BLM and county roads connected to channels in McElmo, Chinle, and lower Montezuma
note: Plan: about 33% less sediment from graveled travel ways

practice: Road surfacing with ditch protection
priority_area: BLM and county roads connected to channels in McElmo, Chinle, and lower Montezuma
note: Plan: about 57% less sediment with travel way and ditch protected; about 91% when the cutslope is also protected

practice: Recreation site sanitation and trail or campsite closure (river corridor, Comb Wash, Cedar Mesa)
priority_area: San Juan corridor; Bears Ears canyons
note: Vault toilets, groover stations, closures and rerouting. Needs BLM, NPS, or Navajo Nation approvals.

practice: Oil and gas pad, pipeline corridor, and access road reclamation (orphaned sites)
priority_area: Aneth and Montezuma Creek oil fields
note: Recontouring, ripping, and seeding of abandoned pads and corridors. Operators are responsible for active and bonded sites, so 319 funding fits only orphaned sites. Produced-water spills add salt.

practice: Canal or ditch piping
priority_area: Irrigated valleys; McElmo salinity hotspots; Indian Creek to Dry Wash
note: Salinity and selenium ratings follow Colorado River Basin Salinity Control Program practice; canal seepage through Mancos Shale is a main selenium source.

practice: Canal or ditch lining
priority_area: Irrigated valleys; McElmo salinity hotspots; Indian Creek to Dry Wash

practice: Sprinkler or drip irrigation conversion
priority_area: Lower Montezuma Creek and other selenium-prone irrigated valleys

practice: Irrigation water management and tailwater reuse
priority_area: Lower Montezuma Creek and other selenium-prone irrigated valleys
note: Carries KWRI R-6 capture-and-reuse ratings

practice: Cover crops and contour farming on irrigated fields
priority_area: Irrigated field margins in McElmo, Chinle, and lower Montezuma
note: Plan: 22-100% sediment reduction for cover crops, depending on establishment; field margins in McElmo, Chinle, and lower Montezuma

practice: Gypsum soil amendment in selenium-prone irrigated fields
priority_area: Selenium-prone irrigated valleys
note: Plan: kept as a candidate, but no transferable efficiency found; use where local soil chemistry supports it

practice: Soil health system: reduced tillage, compost, and residue mulch
priority_area: Irrigated and dryland fields in McElmo, Montezuma, and Recapture valleys
note: Regenerative practice; holds soil moisture and cuts irrigation need. Mulch helped revegetation more than compost on a semiarid rangeland

practice: Runoff (floodwater) farming and water spreading with drought-adapted crops
priority_area: Fields below washes in Chinle, McElmo, and Montezuma Creek (Navajo Nation lands)
note: Traditional dryland farming using brush and rock structures to spread wash flow onto fields; Black Mesa work restored 56 fields. Ratings to be confirmed with farmers and chapters. Discount matched to waterspreading (C-16).

practice: Irrigation flow measurement and diversion control structures
priority_area: Irrigated valleys; McElmo and lower Montezuma Creek
note: NRCS 587 and flow meters. Supports salinity and water-use goals; Utah water optimization funding often applies.

practice: Diversions and water and sediment control basins on dryland fields
priority_area: Blanding and Monticello dryland farms
note: NRCS 362 and 638 (Utah NPS plan Appendix A). Field-scale drainages, so failure risk is lower than in-channel earthen structures. Earthen embankments on field-scale drainages; discount set at 25%, as for waterspreading.

practice: Wind erosion control on fields: windbreaks, cross-wind strips, surface roughening, and residue
priority_area: Dryland fields around Blanding and Monticello; Navajo Nation fields
note: NRCS 380, 589C, 609. Blown soil settles in washes and reaches the river in the next storm. 10% discount because windbreak trees need watering to establish; roughening and residue need none.

practice: Biochar, compost, and other organic soil amendments for water holding
priority_area: Irrigated and dryland fields; small community farms
note: NRCS 336 (soil carbon amendment). Raises water holding in sandy soils, so fields need less irrigation; biochar also binds some metals. Can be made from pinyon-juniper thinning slash. Biochar can raise pH in already alkaline soils, so use low-ash biochar mixed with compost; results in arid alkaline soils are mixed, so ratings are cautious.

practice: Retiring irrigation on saline, selenium-rich fields, with conservation cover
priority_area: McElmo salinity hotspots; lower Montezuma Creek irrigated valleys
note: NRCS 327 (conservation cover). The most direct fix for the worst salt and selenium fields in Colorado River selenium programs. Lost farm income and Utah water right nonuse rules are the main barriers; check the water right before fallowing. Cover is hard to establish on saline soil.

practice: Mine waste cover and revegetation: soil cover and seeding
funding_guide: Legacy mine site cleanup (uranium and metals)
priority_area: Abandoned uranium mine clusters (Four Corners); Cottonwood Wash; White Mesa Mill vicinity
note: Site-specific; usually needs EPA or tribal EPA oversight

practice: Mine waste cover and revegetation: engineered cap
funding_guide: Legacy mine site cleanup (uranium and metals)

note: Radon and erosion barrier; typically outside 319 funding

practice: Run-on diversion and runoff controls at mine sites

practice: Removal and consolidation of mine waste to a repository
funding_guide: Legacy mine site cleanup (uranium and metals)
priority_area: Abandoned uranium mine clusters (Four Corners)
note: Usually Superfund or abandoned-mine program scale

practice: Passive selenium treatment: constructed wetland
funding_guide: Legacy mine site cleanup (uranium and metals)
priority_area: Selenium-bearing drainages in lower Montezuma Creek
tracking_unit: Treatment cells installed or discharges treated
note: Plan: 56-70% selenium mass removal and over 94% suspended sediment retention. Needs a persistent, identifiable drainage. Birds can take up selenium in treatment wetlands, so negative impacts are rated higher.

practice: Passive selenium treatment: bioreactor
funding_guide: Legacy mine site cleanup (uranium and metals)
priority_area: Selenium-bearing drainages in lower Montezuma Creek
tracking_unit: Treatment cells installed or discharges treated
note: Plan: about 70% selenium removal; sensitive to residence time and temperature. Only where flow is focused and reliable

practice: Groundwater interception and treatment for uranium (reactive media or pump and treat)
funding_guide: Legacy mine site cleanup (uranium and metals)
priority_area: White Mesa Mill vicinity; confirmed groundwater pathways
note: Outside Utah's NPS program: the abandoned mines plan funds passive treatment only. Plan example: Monticello mill site system cut uranium from about 300 micrograms per liter to below the 44 microgram per liter groundwater standard. Only after source verification and regulatory coordination

practice: Septic system: pumping and repair
priority_area: Lower Montezuma Creek communities; unsewered areas
tracking_unit: Systems repaired or replaced; households connected

practice: Septic system: replacement
priority_area: Lower Montezuma Creek communities; unsewered areas
tracking_unit: Systems repaired or replaced; households connected

practice: Septic system: advanced treatment
priority_area: Lower Montezuma Creek communities; unsewered areas
tracking_unit: Systems repaired or replaced; households connected

practice: Septic system: connection to a cluster or community system
priority_area: Lower Montezuma Creek communities; unsewered areas
tracking_unit: Systems repaired or replaced; households connected
note: Plan: 85% bacteria reduction after community-wide septic replacement and rehabilitation

practice: Outhouse and pit privy replacement (vault or composting toilets)
priority_area: Homes without indoor plumbing near wells and washes
note: Many homes on the Navajo Nation have no indoor plumbing. Unlined pits near wells and washes are an E. coli and nitrate source. Composting toilets need no water.

practice: Drinking water line extension
priority_area: Not a plan priority area; homes on unregulated wells
note: No in-stream load reduction; benefit is lower exposure to uranium and arsenic in unregulated wells

practice: Uranium and arsenic treatment for individual wells (point-of-entry or point-of-use)
priority_area: Not a plan priority area; homes on unregulated wells
note: Reverse osmosis or adsorptive media at the tap or where water enters the home. Needs regular filter changes, testing, and safe disposal of spent media. Protects people, not streams, so Environmental is 0.

practice: Uranium or arsenic treatment: community system
priority_area: Not a plan priority area; homes on unregulated wells
note: No in-stream load reduction

practice: Uranium and arsenic treatment: community water filling station
priority_area: Not a plan priority area; chapter communities with hauled water
note: Treated water for families who haul water from unregulated wells. Protects people, not streams.

practice: Wastewater lagoon or treatment plant improvement
priority_area: Not a plan priority area; community lagoons
note: Point source; included because it is in the Funding Guide

practice: Stormwater harvesting basins: lot-scale (homes, chapter houses, schools)
priority_area: Not a plan priority area; Bluff, Blanding, Monticello, chapter communities
note: Tucson-style passive water harvesting. Metals lowered: Phoenix-area bioswales removed about 25% of heavy metals

practice: Stormwater harvesting basins: street-side with curb cuts
priority_area: Not a plan priority area; Bluff, Blanding, Monticello, chapter communities
note: Needs city or UDOT approval

practice: Vegetated swale with desert plantings
priority_area: Not a plan priority area; Bluff, Blanding, Monticello, chapter communities
note: Phoenix-area bioswales removed 76-99% of suspended solids and about 25% of heavy metals

practice: Rainwater cisterns
priority_area: Not a plan priority area; Bluff, Blanding, Monticello, chapter communities

practice: Small community and backyard farms: drip, mulch, and compost
priority_area: Chapter communities, Bluff, Blanding, Monticello
note: Cuts water use and runoff from small farms and gardens

practice: Backyard livestock pen and manure management near wells and washes
priority_area: Lower Montezuma Creek communities; homes near washes
note: Scaled-down corral runoff control (G-5) for household animals

practice: Well and wellhead protection (sealing, setbacks from corrals and septic)
priority_area: Homes and livestock wells; White Mesa and chapter communities
note: Protects groundwater rather than streams; most benefit is to drinking water

practice: Abandoned well decommissioning (plugging and sealing)
priority_area: Homes and livestock wells; White Mesa and chapter communities
note: NRCS 351 (well decommissioning). Closes a direct path for surface runoff, manure, and septic effluent into groundwater, and removes a safety hazard. Needs a licensed driller.

practice: Private and livestock well testing (uranium, arsenic, E. coli, nitrate)
priority_area: Homes and livestock wells; White Mesa and chapter communities
note: NRCS 355 (well water testing). Screening, not treatment: tells families and partners where treatment, wellhead protection, or decommissioning is needed. Environmental is 0 because testing changes no load. Retest every 1 to 2 years.

practice: Spring development with protection and overflow returned
priority_area: Abajo headwaters and foothill springs; Bears Ears springs
note: Return overflow to keep spring habitat wet

practice: Spring and seep and wet meadow restoration
priority_area: Abajo headwater meadows; Bears Ears springs
note: Exclosure plus one-rock dams and rundowns and induced meandering

practice: Headwater tributary exclosure (livestock and elk)
priority_area: Abajo headwater streams
note: Elk-proof fence costs more

practice: Forest road drainage and stream crossing upgrades
priority_area: Abajo Mountains headwaters (Manti-La Sal NF)
note: Includes aquatic organism passage culverts

practice: Fuels reduction thinning and prescribed fire
priority_area: Abajo Mountains headwaters (Manti-La Sal NF)
note: Benefit is avoided post-fire sediment

practice: Post-fire stabilization: mulching and seeding
priority_area: Burned areas connected to priority waters (Abajo, Bears Ears)
note: Post-fire BMP tool (Lay 2026), 11-20 inch rainfall class used for most Abajo burns: mulching about 18 of 20 and seeding 15, the top hillslope treatments. A 222-observation meta-analysis agrees mulch works best; the effect fades as plants recover.

practice: Post-fire stabilization: log erosion barriers
priority_area: Burned areas connected to priority waters (Abajo, Bears Ears)
note: Post-fire BMP tool (Lay 2026), 11-20 inch rainfall class used for most Abajo burns: contour felling and log terraces about 8 of 20 (4 where rainfall is under 10 inches), so ratings stay low.

practice: Post-fire stabilization: contour raking or ripping with seeding
priority_area: Burned areas connected to priority waters (Abajo, Bears Ears)
note: Post-fire BMP tool (Lay 2026), 11-20 inch rainfall class used for most Abajo burns: hand raking and contour ripping about 18 of 20, tied with mulching. Pair with seeding.

practice: Post-fire stabilization: straw wattles, fiber logs, and erosion control blankets
priority_area: Burned areas connected to priority waters (Abajo, Bears Ears)
note: Post-fire BMP tool (Lay 2026), 11-20 inch rainfall class: blankets about 17 of 20, wattles and fiber logs 12 to 13, below mulching and raking (18) and above log terraces (8). Plastic netting can trap wildlife; use wildlife-safe products.

practice: Aspen and riparian woody protection from browsing
priority_area: Abajo Mountains headwaters

practice: Streamside management zones during forest work (75 ft perennial, 35 ft intermittent)
funding_guide: Riparian restoration; Fuels reduction or prescribed fire
priority_area: Abajo Mountains
note: Forest operations only (fuels, salvage, harvest). Widths from Utah Forest Water Quality Guidelines for slopes under 35%. Utah BMP Selector UT-FOR-07, its top practice.

practice: Skid trail and landing rehabilitation
funding_guide: Erosion control or stream stabilization; Fuels reduction or prescribed fire
priority_area: Abajo Mountains
note: Forest operations only. Waterbars, ripping, slash cover, seeding (NRCS 654 partial, 342).

practice: Induced meandering and wicker weirs in small creeks
priority_area: Abajo Mountains
note: Zeedyk-style. Fits small Abajo creeks and spring-fed channels with willow nearby; likely to blow out in large sandy washes.

practice: Spring and seep exclosures (livestock, elk, and feral horses)
priority_area: Abajo headwaters and foothill springs; Bears Ears springs
note: Fencing alone, without spring development. Pipe overflow to a trough outside the fence (F-1) so animals still have water; otherwise the negative-impact rating drops.
